content:
# Sirach 49 — Disagreement Log

**Chapter:** Sirach 49 | **Date:** 2026-03-17 | **Total Disagreements:** 15

---

## Disagreement 1 — 49:1, "blending of incense" — the opening simile

**EMET:** "like a blending of incense, prepared by the work of the perfumer"
**LOGOS:** "like a blending of incense skillfully prepared"
**PNEUMA:** "like perfectly blended incense"
**Issue:** Greek hōs miama thurmiamatos = like a mixture of incense. "Prepared by the work of the perfumer" (EMET) retains the craftsman reference. LOGOS compresses; PNEUMA loses the craftsman entirely.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA retains the full phrase "prepared by the work of the perfumer" — the skilled artisan is part of the simile.

---

## Disagreement 2 — 49:2, "conversion" vs. "turning" vs. "turning the people back"

**EMET:** "the conversion of the people"
**LOGOS:** "the conversion of the people"
**PNEUMA:** "turning the people back"
**Issue:** Greek epistrophē laou = turning of the people. "Conversion" (EMET/LOGOS) has too-Christian a connotation in English; "turning back" (PNEUMA) is more literal.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "the conversion of the people" — in the LXX context "conversion" means return to proper observance, which is accurate for Josiah's reform.

---

## Disagreement 3 — 49:2, "abominations of lawlessness" vs. "abominations of iniquity"

**EMET:** "the abominations of lawlessness"
**LOGOS:** "the abominations of iniquity"
**PNEUMA:** "the abominations of sin"
**Issue:** Greek bdelugmata anomias = abominations of lawlessness. "Lawlessness" (EMET) is most literal; "iniquity" (LOGOS) is more traditional.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA retains "abominations of lawlessness" — anomia = lawlessness specifically (not just sin).

---

## Disagreement 4 — 49:3, "confirmed piety" vs. "upheld piety" vs. "made piety take root"

**EMET:** "he confirmed piety"
**LOGOS:** "he upheld piety"
**PNEUMA:** "he made piety take root"
**Issue:** Greek kateuqynen eusebeia = he directed/established piety. "Confirmed" (EMET) and "upheld" (LOGOS) both work; PNEUMA's "take root" is a botanical metaphor without support.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "he confirmed piety" — most literal.

---

## Disagreement 5 — 49:4, "all committed great offenses" vs. "all were gravely at fault"

**EMET:** "all committed great offenses"
**LOGOS:** "all were gravely at fault"
**PNEUMA:** "all the kings of Judah sinned greatly"
**Issue:** Greek hyperthumōs ēmarton = they sinned exceedingly/greatly. EMET "committed great offenses" is literal; LOGOS "gravely at fault" is somewhat softened.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "all committed great offenses."

---

## Disagreement 6 — 49:4, "failed to the very last" vs. "came to ruin at the end"

**EMET:** "the kings of Judah failed to the very last"
**LOGOS:** "the kings of Judah came to ruin at the end"
**PNEUMA:** "they came to ruin, every last one"
**Issue:** Greek basileiai Iouda edōkan to keras = the kingdoms of Judah gave the horn (i.e., gave up their power/glory). "Failed" (EMET) and "came to ruin" (LOGOS) both capture the sense of ultimate defeat.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "the kings of Judah failed to the very last" — "to the very last" has the right finality.

---

## Disagreement 7 — 49:6, "who set fire to" vs. "who burned"

**EMET:** "who set fire to the chosen city of the sanctuary"
**LOGOS:** "who burned the chosen city of the sanctuary"
**PNEUMA:** "who burned the holy city, the city God had chosen"
**Issue:** Greek enepyrisan = set fire to, burned. EMET "set fire to" is slightly more active/dramatic; "burned" (LOGOS) is more concise.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "who set fire to the chosen city of the sanctuary."

---

## Disagreement 8 — 49:7, "pull up and to afflict" vs. "pull up and tear down"

**EMET:** "to pull up and to afflict and to destroy"
**LOGOS:** "to pull up and tear down and destroy"
**PNEUMA:** "to uproot and tear down and destroy"
**Issue:** Greek katarrizoun kai kathairein = to root up and to pull down. Jeremiah 1:10 LXX has "to root out and to demolish and to destroy." LOGOS/PNEUMA align with Jer. 1:10; EMET uses "afflict" for kathairein which is incorrect.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "to pull up and to tear down and to destroy" — aligning with the Jeremiah citation.

---

## Disagreement 9 — 49:8, "chariot of the cherubim" vs. "cherubim-throne"

**EMET:** "over the chariot of the cherubim"
**LOGOS:** "above the chariot of the cherubim"
**PNEUMA:** "above the cherubim-throne"
**Issue:** Greek harma = chariot, the merkavah. "Chariot" must be preserved — PNEUMA's "throne" loses the chariot imagery central to Ezekiel 1.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA retains "chariot of the cherubim."

---

## Disagreement 10 — 49:9, "he also mentioned Job" — attribution

**EMET:** "For he also mentioned Job"
**LOGOS:** "For he also referred to Job"
**PNEUMA:** "He also mentioned Job"
**Issue:** Greek emnēsthē = he remembered/mentioned. The subject is Ezekiel (v. 8). All agents agree this is Ezekiel mentioning Job (Ezek. 14). "Mentioned" (EMET/PNEUMA) vs. "referred to" (LOGOS).
**Resolution:** SOPHIA follows EMET: "he also mentioned Job."

---

## Disagreement 11 — 49:10, "sprout again" vs. "spring up fresh" vs. "bud fresh"

**EMET:** "may their bones sprout again from their places"
**LOGOS:** "may their bones spring up fresh from where they lie"
**PNEUMA:** "may the bones of the Twelve Prophets bud fresh from where they rest"
**Issue:** Greek anatolēsai = to sprout, spring up, arise. "Sprout again" (EMET) and "spring up fresh" (LOGOS) are close. The botanical metaphor of new growth from buried bones should be preserved.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "may the bones of the twelve prophets sprout anew from where they lie" — combining EMET/LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 12 — 49:11, "How shall we magnify" vs. "How are we to extol"

**EMET:** "How shall we magnify Zerubbabel?"
**LOGOS:** "How are we to extol Zerubbabel?"
**PNEUMA:** "What words are big enough for Zerubbabel?"
**Issue:** Greek megalunōmen = let us magnify/exalt. Rhetorical question implying his greatness cannot be fully expressed. EMET/LOGOS are close; PNEUMA paraphrases.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "How shall we magnify Zerubbabel?" — the verb "magnify" has liturgical resonance (cf. Magnificat).

---

## Disagreement 13 — 49:13, "raised up for us the walls that had fallen" vs. "rebuilt our fallen walls"

**EMET:** "he raised up for us the walls that had fallen"
**LOGOS:** "he rebuilt for us the fallen walls"
**PNEUMA:** "he rebuilt our fallen walls"
**Issue:** Greek anistesin hēmin teichē peptōkota = he raised up for us the walls that had fallen. EMET's "raised up" is more literal and more elevated; LOGOS "rebuilt" is more common English.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "he rebuilt for us the walls that had fallen" — "rebuilt" is more natural; "that had fallen" preserves the participle.

---

## Disagreement 14 — 49:15, "and his body was cared for" vs. "his body was kept watch over"

**EMET:** "and his body was cared for"
**LOGOS:** "and his body was watched over"
**PNEUMA:** "and even his body was kept from decay"
**Issue:** Greek sōma autou epeskephthē = his body was visited/attended. The reference is to Joseph's bones being carried from Egypt (Gen. 50:25–26; Josh. 24:32). "Watched over" (LOGOS) is more literal; PNEUMA adds "decay" which is not in the text.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "his body was kept watch over" (LOGOS) — the ongoing guardianship of Joseph's remains.

---

## Disagreement 15 — 49:16, Adam as climax

**EMET:** "above every living thing was Adam in his creation"
**LOGOS:** "above every living being in the creation was Adam"
**PNEUMA:** "Adam, in his creation, stood above all living things"
**Issue:** Greek kai uper pan zōon en tē ktisei Adaam = and above every living thing in the creation was Adam. The word order of LOGOS preserves the Greek more exactly; PNEUMA adds "stood." The climactic position of Adam must be honored.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "but above every living thing in creation was Adam" — a small change from LOGOS, retaining the Greek word order with the strong adversative "but."

---

*Total disagreements logged: 15*
